title: YAGA Q&A — Creator/Writer/Showrunner Kat Sandler on the Thrill of Entering the Global Stage
summary: We sat down with YAGA creator/writer/showrunner Kat Sandler to discuss the seeds of her original play, what she thinks today’s audiences are craving, and her excitement around YAGA’s exposure to a global audience.
body_markdown:
*YAGA* has everyone on the edge of their seats, and with only two episodes left, things are only going to get crazier. In this psychological descent into witchcraft and seductions, two investigators unlock dark secrets after questioning a mysterious professor (Carrie-Ann Moss) about a missing student (Hudson Williams). We sat down with *YAGA* creator/writer/showrunner Kat Sandler to discuss the seeds of her original play, what she thinks today’s audiences are craving, and her excitement around *YAGA* ’s exposure to a global audience.


**I really want to start at the beginning. How did the seeds for your play** ***YAGA*** **really get sown? Did you have an interest in folklore in general? Did you grow up hearing this specific Slavic folklore – where did your interest in all of this really begin?**


So, I had asthma as a kid and my mom would always read to me. My mom was a writer and I got really, really obsessed with fairytales. Of course, I was a big Disney kid. I loved everything about the world of fairytales, princesses and princes, witches and monsters. It was really fascinating to me as a kid, and I think that’s stayed with me my whole life.


As I got older, it became glaringly apparent that the princesses were having the least fun out of everybody in those stories. It seemed like their whole existence was just to get rescued, get married and have as many babies as humanly possible. The witches and the villains were actually way more interesting and complex, so those stories started to mean a lot more to me.


I don't remember the first time I ever heard the Baba Yaga story, but I remember being really taken with just how striking the imagery of it was. I'm a really visual person and the idea of a hut that can move around on chicken feet and a witch whose primary mode of transportation is a mortar and pestle that flies through the sky and then grinds the bones of naughty children was *really* fascinating.


Also, I loved the fact that she had a name at all! So often witches are just ‘the wicked old witch’ or ‘the one from Hansel and Gretel’ or the ‘Wicked Witch of the West’ before we had Elphaba. They’ve really been nameless. I think that's just a hallmark of the way that we write women out of history and stories, even fairytales! So, it was really striking that she had this name, Baba Yaga.


I used to write a lot of these really complex, funny male characters when I was younger, because I thought it probably wasn't very cool to be a feminist. And as I got older, I was like, "Oh, actually it’s very, very cool and women are just endlessly more interesting." Really focusing on the way that society villainizes women and asking the questions, “what makes a monster?” and “what makes a witch?” We answer that in the show, with "a witch is just somebody society has decided it's afraid of for whatever reason."


**The idea of transforming a play into a television series is exciting but also seems incredibly daunting. When did the conversation around turning your play into a show really begin and how does one try and tackle that transformation, especially in those early days?**


It really started with our executive producer, Mackenzie Donaldson. She had been asked by the executives at Bell if she had any ideas for a half hour drama, and she had seen the play in its original run. She called me and asked me if I thought it could be a TV show, and I said, "F*ck, of course." Like, in theater, I write and direct. I think almost every single play I've ever had produced, I've also directed. So, the process of show running is actually very similar to writing and directing a theater production. You're building a world and you're populating it and finding all the pieces. You’re working with other artists to pull that story out of your head and onto a stage.


I’ve worked in television before, mostly in development. I've been in a couple rooms, but never on this scale. My writing is very fast paced; it's really high stakes. It's really darkly funny all the time. I can't not make a joke. So, those moments that you've seen where you're in a morgue and then someone makes a dick joke and you're like, "Oh, well, there it is." The comedy is a release valve for me.


So, while it was daunting, I think I was made to do this. We had an amazing group in the room. I had one of the original dramaturges from the play, the person who co-founded my theater company with me, people that I've collected from that side of my career, and then a bunch of TV people that really helped shift it. It was about getting the right people in the room and being like, "What do you want the experience of the audience to be?"


That's the way that I've always made theater. It's always a conversation with the audience. What's so cool about *YAGA* is that I've been having this conversation in different forms for basically 10 years. This play has been performed all over Canada and the States. I learn something every time from the way an audience reacts to it. So, it's just about what you want an audience to take away and how you can challenge them. Audiences are so smart now. They have access to so much story, and I think they really want to sit up and pay attention and engage with the thing you're presenting them with.


**The casting for the show is just absolutely spot on and features such an amazing group of Canadian actors like Sheila McCarthy & Megan Fellows. I know Noah Reid was involved with workshops of the original play, which is SO cool, so he was a given! How involved were you in casting for the show?**


Incredibly involved! I cast it with Mackenzie in conversation with Blink49 and Crave executives.


**There are so many different elements that are being explored in the show — obsession, sexuality, friendship, religious fervor, social norms, gender norms — did opening this up into a TV series allow you to dig into certain areas a bit more than what had been explored in the play?**


Expanding to TV allows you to show more without telling; you can do with a look in a closeup what you might need a monologue to do in a play, so it was really exciting to get to dig down into the emotions of the characters, and the characters themselves.


In the play, 3 actors played all the characters; the same actor who played Rapp played Henry, the same actor playing Katherine played Geena, so it was exciting to break them out and give them their own lives, motivations and conflicts.


**What’s been the most exciting thing for you as a creator with this project? The exposure to American audiences must be exciting — as a fellow Canadian I love to see Canadians gain notoriety in the States. Having more eyeballs on your art can also be intense though! What are you hoping audiences come away with after watching** ***YAGA*** **?**


It’s a cliché, but the thing I’m most excited for is seeing it come to life in this new format and getting to have built it alongside this brilliant team.


And it’s already intense! But we’re incredibly grateful to have these eyes on us in an insanely competitive time for original content. We’ve always said that we wanted *YAGA* to be an epically Canadian show with global ambition, and now we’ve sold to streamers in countries all over the world. From our iconic, generation-spanning cast, to the stunning British Columbia landscapes we get to showcase, to the fact that this story began as a play in a 200-seat theatre in Toronto and was born out of Canadian theatre and storytelling, it feels like a dream come true to see *YAGA* reach this kind of audience.


We’re coming hot on the heels of the inspirational success of *Heated Rivalry* , and it’s so clear that Canadian art is raring to take up space. It’s a gift to present something about female empowerment, that is unapologetically weird, fun and freaky, angry and Canadian at its core, and have audiences around the world pay attention. I hope viewers will go on this wild ride with us and be surprised, challenged, and above all, entertained.
